extracted.intended_audience: authors, reviewers, editors and staff of Royal Society journals (research authors and peer reviewers)
extracted.subtask_description: Publisher-level editorial and peer review standards for Royal Society research journals covering editorial independence, peer review models, co-reviewing, appeals, corrections/retractions, author name changes, and comment/reply rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial independence
rubrics_metrics.description: Editorial independence is respected. The content of Royal Society journals is entirely independent of the Society’s views on any scientific or policy issues. The editor’s decision is final and will not be influenced or compromised in any way by the Society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors' decisions stand independently of the Society; editorial independence must be maintained in all decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer review system (anonymity model)
rubrics_metrics.description: Most papers are peer reviewed in a single-anonymized fashion (author names are not concealed, but referee names are); Notes and Records and Proceedings B are double-anonymized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware which journals use single- vs double-anonymized review; procedures and expectations may differ by journal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measures to minimise bias in peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: We do all we can to ensure the peer review process is fair and we aim to minimise bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measures include: striving for diverse representation on editorial boards; encouraging board members to select reviewers from a diverse pool (including author suggestions); regular reminders to board members, reviewers and staff about unconscious biases; working with other publishers to collect anonymised diversity data to assess potential biases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transfer of peer-reviewed preprints (Review Commons)
rubrics_metrics.description: Open Biology accepts the transfer of peer-reviewed preprints directly from the Review Commons online portal into the editorial workflow, where they are assessed for publication without restarting the peer review process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors can transfer peer-reviewed preprints into the submission workflow for relevant journals to avoid restarting peer review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication of peer review information (transparent peer review policy)
rubrics_metrics.description: For Royal Society Open Science, Open Biology and Proceedings B, publication of peer review information (anonymous by default unless the reviewer signs their report) is mandatory. For Proceedings A and Biology Letters, authors are offered the option to publish peer review information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Referee reports and correspondence remain confidential unless published with the article; journals differ on mandatory vs optional transparent peer review—check journal-specific policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality of referee reports and correspondence
rubrics_metrics.description: Unless published with the article, the referee reports and other correspondence relating to your paper must remain confidential and should not be shared or made publicly available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discussions between author, editor and referee that have taken place in confidence will remain so unless explicit consent is given by all parties or there are exceptional circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on inputting manuscript details into generative AI tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Referees inputting manuscript details into generative AI tools is prohibited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AI tools provide no guarantee of where data are being sent, saved, viewed, or used in the future; therefore manuscript details must not be fed into such tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling editor conflicts of interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors or board members are never involved in editorial decisions about their own work and in these cases papers may be referred to other editors or the editor-in-chief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When editors have a conflict, referral to alternate editors ensures impartial handling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Edits to reviewer reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Edits to reviews are kept to an absolute minimum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Edits address only issues of tone, language, and deviations from journal policy and reviewer guidelines, and will not change the meaning or intention of the review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abusive behaviour policy toward staff and participants
rubrics_metrics.description: The Royal Society does not tolerate abusive behaviour or correspondence towards its staff, academic editors, authors or reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any author engaging in abusive behaviour will have their paper immediately withdrawn from consideration; consideration of subsequent submissions is at the Editor's discretion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Co-reviewing policy and accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: A co-reviewer is a researcher or technician who reviews a manuscript together with a more senior (invited) reviewer. The senior reviewer is limited to one appropriately qualified co-reviewer per review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The review process is confidential. To provide accountability and credit, the name and status (e.g. PhD student) of the co-reviewer should be disclosed on submission of the review. The senior reviewer is the main point of contact and is ultimately accountable; senior reviewer and co-reviewer should agree on wording. Confidentiality and competing interest principles apply equally. Where peer review information is published, senior reviewers may disclose their name and may include a co-reviewer’s name if the co-reviewer consents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeals process for editorial decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors have a right to appeal editorial decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should submit grounds for appeal to the editorial office, addressed to the editor; they are discouraged from directly contacting editorial board members. Following an appeal, all editorial decisions are final. Editors will mediate exchanges between authors and referees and may invite additional referees where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to correct the literature
rubrics_metrics.description: The journal has a responsibility for the accuracy and reliability of the research it publishes and a duty to correct the literature when appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corrections are achieved by publication of specific article types (expression of concern, correction, retraction, addendum, editor’s note) depending on the issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expression of concern (use and timing)
rubrics_metrics.description: An expression of concern is used to make readers aware that the journal has concerns about the accuracy of an article and that it is currently being investigated or evaluated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normally in effect during the decision-making/investigation process; may be issued when investigations are lengthy or ambiguous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correction (when appropriate)
rubrics_metrics.description: A correction is normally used when a small portion of an otherwise reliable publication proves to be misleading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Errors requiring correction include: anything that changes data or the scientific meaning; anything in metadata elements (title, authors, affiliations, funding info); any other error where it is imperative that all readers and downstream vendors have the updated version.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retraction (criteria)
rubrics_metrics.description: A retraction is a notification of invalid results and/or conclusions and will be considered if editors have clear evidence that the findings are unreliable (due to misconduct or honest error); if the findings have been previously published elsewhere without proper cross-referencing (redundant publication); it constitutes plagiarism; or it reports unethical research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retraction is used where findings are invalid and may invalidate conclusions; follow COPE guidance and ensure timely action if appropriate and if authors do not respond satisfactorily.

rubrics_metrics.name: Addendum and editor's note (uses)
rubrics_metrics.description: An addendum can provide additional information or clarification; an editor’s note is a less formal communication to draw attention to a particular aspect of an article when other article types are not appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Addenda focus on what needs changing or clarifying and are not a forum for debate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Format and publication of notices (correction/expression/retraction/addendum)
rubrics_metrics.description: Notices are written so readers can identify and understand the correction or reason for retraction; notices have their own DOI but are linked electronically with the original publication; the original article remains online with the notice linked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notices are published in a form that enables indexing and abstracting services to identify and link corrections and retractions; published at the end of the latest issue and appear on the table of contents. A retraction must be authored by the author, the author's legal counsel, the author's sponsoring institution, the editorial office or the editor. Retracted articles remain on the website but are clearly marked and the PDF carries a watermark on every page. The Royal Society uses CrossMark to indicate document status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Process for handling allegations about research integrity
rubrics_metrics.description: Concerns can be raised by anyone (anonymously or publicly). Allegations are brought to the Editor-in-Chief who acknowledges receipt and asks for supporting evidence; allegations are shared with authors who are asked for their response while respecting confidentiality requests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should follow COPE flowcharts. The investigation aims to determine the integrity/reliability of the published research, not the integrity of the individual author(s). Investigations vary in complexity and may involve committees, other journals, legal representatives, institutions and the publisher’s communications team. If an investigation is lengthy an expression of concern may be issued. Before action, findings are reviewed with the publishing team for consistent approach; final decision communicated to authors and relevant bodies; retraction notice posted online and in next issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author name change policy after publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors may change their name for many reasons and the Royal Society facilitates changes to author names, email addresses, biography photos, pronouns, and other identifiers as necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Changes are made directly to the article PDF and HTML; metadata are re-sent to abstracting and indexing services (though the publisher cannot enforce replacement on those platforms). The DOI remains the same. The Royal Society retains an original version in a secure environment but it is not publicly available. Authors should contact the editorial office to request changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open criticism and debate policy
rubrics_metrics.description: The Society encourages academic debate and constructive criticism of research. Authors do not have a right to veto unfavourable comments about their work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No referee comment or published correspondence may contain a personal attack on any of the authors. Criticism should target the work (not the researcher). Editors should edit or reject personal or offensive statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comment and reply policy (scope and process)
rubrics_metrics.description: A comment brings attention to an oversight or proposes an opposing view and is often a critique providing corrections or new analyses. A comment is not used to address ethical issues (use COPE guidelines instead).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A comment can be proposed by any reader within three months of online publication of the article and is published at the Editor's discretion. The comment is peer-reviewed (usually by a referee from the original article and another impartial referee) and shared with the corresponding author. If accepted, it is held to allow a reply from the original authors. The reply will also be peer-reviewed (if it passes triage). Comment and reply is normally limited to one round.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition for reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: The Royal Society provides recognition for reviewing Royal Society journal articles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See journal 'Information for Reviewers' for details of reviewer recognition and related guidance.
